title: Minimum Number of Changes to Make Binary String Beautiful
statement: You are given a binary string `s` whose length is even. The string is **beautiful** when it can be cut into one or more consecutive pieces such that every piece has an even length and is made of a single repeated character (all `'0'` or all `'1'`). In one change you may set any single character of `s` to `'0'` or `'1'`. Return the fewest changes that make `s` beautiful.
constraints: s contains only the characters '0' and '1'
notes:
## Intuition

Any even-length block of one character can itself be cut into blocks of length exactly 2. So a string is beautiful exactly when every aligned pair `s[0..1]`, `s[2..3]`, ... holds two equal characters. The pairs do not interact: fixing one pair never helps or hurts another. A pair that already matches costs nothing, and a pair like `"01"` needs exactly one change (either character can be flipped). Greedily fixing each pair on its own is therefore optimal.

A brute force would try every binary string of the same length, keep the beautiful ones and measure how many positions differ, which is exponential.

## Approach

1. Set `changes = 0`.
2. Step `i` through `0, 2, 4, ...`, reading the pair `first = s[i]` and `second = s[i + 1]`.
3. If they differ, one change is needed for this pair, so add 1 to `changes`.
4. Return `changes`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "1001"`. The pairs are `"10"` and `"01"`.

- `i = 0`: `first = '1'`, `second = '0'` differ, so `changes = 1`.
- `i = 2`: `first = '0'`, `second = '1'` differ, so `changes = 2`.

The answer is `2` (for example `"1100"` or `"0000"`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is read once.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Pairs must be aligned at even indices; comparing every neighbour `s[i]`, `s[i + 1]` for all `i` counts the wrong boundaries (`"0011"` needs no change even though its middle neighbours differ).
- Counting odd-length runs is not the answer: `"1000"` has two odd runs but needs only one change.
- A mismatched pair costs exactly one change, never two.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `changes` | number of changes made so far |
| `i` | index of the first character of the current pair |
| `first`, `second` | the two characters of the current pair |

narration.2: No characters have been changed yet.
narration.3: Visit the string two characters at a time, in aligned pairs.
narration.4: Read the first character of the pair...
narration.6: A pair with two different characters cannot be part of any uniform even block.
narration.7: Changing either character fixes it, so this pair costs exactly one change.
narration.10: Every pair is now uniform, so the string is beautiful; return the count.
